column4: It asks exactly what the Day of Recompense (يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ) is, opening the same event named in 1:4.
The repeated question about يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ makes the day an overwhelming occurrence rather than an ordinary date.
On that day no soul can possess or do anything for another, and the command belongs to Allah; this unfolds the exclusive Mālik of 1:4.
The guarding scribes begin the immediate context of the Day of Recompense: no deed can disappear from its account.
Its noble recorders make concrete the section's reckoning, alongside 82:17-19's Day of Recompense.
They know what people do, supplying the recorded evidence for the recompense named later in the passage.
The righteous are in bliss, one of the two outcomes surrounding the Day of Recompense in 82:17-19.
The wicked are in Hell, the punitive counterpart to the section's account and divine wrath.
They enter it on the Day of Recompense, joining the day directly to its due outcome.
They are not absent from the Fire; the section likewise stresses that no one slips away from that day's settlement.
Its woe to defrauders introduces the crooked commercial scale that reverses the section's full, non-tilting coin.
They demand full measure when receiving, a one-sided counterpart to equal valuation and payment.
When measuring or weighing for others they give less (يُخْسِرُونَ), the inverse of the upright scale tied to مُسْتَقِيم.
The cheaters are asked whether they expect resurrection, explicitly carrying their market fraud into the final account.
It calls that resurrection a عظیم day, the grave event which gives the deficient weighing its final consequence.
People stand (يَقُومُ ٱلنَّاسُ) before the Lord, directly joining the q-w-m family of standing to the Day and the balance scene.
On the day all come forth, ownership is asked and answered: the kingdom belongs to the One, Overpowering Allah.
Each soul is repaid for what it earned, without injustice, and Allah is swift in account; it states the reckoning under 40:16's sole kingship.
The true kingdom on that day belongs to the Merciful, bringing the surah's Rahmān and its Mālik of the Day together.
It gives the prosperous destination of the people of Paradise on the same day whose true dominion 25:26 assigns to the Merciful.
The sky's splitting and the angels' descent stage the Day immediately before 25:26's declaration of true kingship.
Allah sets the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection and brings even a mustard-seed weight: the section's exact, non-leaning balance at final account.
The weighing on that day is truth itself; heavy scales lead to success, directly complementing the full-weight coin.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves, giving the adverse end of deficient weight and misvaluation.
Whoever's scales are heavy succeeds, repeating the final balance with a personal outcome.
Light scales make their possessors lose themselves in Hell, the reversal that makes the upright measure morally consequential.
It explicitly shows the heavy side of the scales (ثَقُلَتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُ), the section's full weight on the favorable side.
The one with heavy scales receives a pleasing life, completing 101:6's recompense.
It explicitly shows the light side of the scales (خَفَّتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُ), the contrary outcome of insufficient weight.
The abyss is assigned to the one with light scales, completing the negative side of the same weighing.
Its question about the abyss intensifies the account's consequence begun by the light scales in 101:8.
The abyss is a blazing fire, the punitive destination tied to the failed balance.
It joins a fixed-term debt, writing, a witness who may forget (تَضِلَّ), and the description أَقْوَمُ for sounder testimony; the section's debt, memory, and q-w-m balance occur together.
A debtor in hardship is granted deferment, making the section's due date and debt settlement a lived ethical scene.
Its pledge, entrusted party, and warning not to conceal testimony extend 2:282's debt contract and accountable witness.
It commands full measure and weighing with the upright balance (ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ), explicitly giving the section's straight path a market scale.
Give full measure and do not cause loss: the command begins the same fair-weighing scene completed by 26:182.
Weigh with the upright balance (ٱلْقِسْطَاسِ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمِ), the exact verbal meeting of the section's straightness and scale.
Do not deprive people of their things or spread corruption; it gives the social wrong that an unequal scale commits.
Allah raised the sky and set the balance (ٱلْمِيزَانَ), enlarging the section's measure from coin to created order.
Do not transgress the balance: its boundary explains why a scale that tips or is manipulated violates the order Allah set.
Establish weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient, the direct opposite of the deficient weighing in 83:3.
The Book and the balance are sent down so people may uphold justice; it states the public purpose of the straight measure.
Give full measure and weight with justice, a direct command for the full and even weighing pictured in the section.
Shu'ayb commands full measure and balance with justice and forbids depriving people of their goods, joining commerce to moral account.
Shu'ayb's warning to Madyan to worship Allah begins the passage whose concrete test is complete measure and balance.
Give full measure and balance with justice and do not diminish people's things, another direct earthly instance of the section's unbent scale.
Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good; exact tiny weight becomes exact recompense.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good sees it, translating final account into the smallest measurable deed.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil sees it, the matching adverse measure.
After intentional killing, pardon requires fair following and gracious payment; it is the qisas-to-payment turn developed under غَيْر.
Retaliation contains life, explaining why the legal equivalence beside 2:178 is neither arbitrary vengeance nor a lost blood claim.
Accidental killing requires a diya delivered to the family, the concrete blood payment named by the section.
Deliberate murder brings Allah's wrath, curse, and great punishment, tying the diya passage to the section's explanation of divine غضب as punishment.
Its life-for-life equivalence and its valuation of forgiveness as charity show retaliation and remission as measured responses.
The slain person's heir receives authority, but must not exceed the limit in killing; it guards against blood being both unavenged and over-avenged.
A soul may be held for what it earned, and no ransom or equivalent payment is accepted from it: substitution fails at the final settlement.
Fear the day when no soul can compensate for another and no ransom or intercession is accepted; it is a direct boundary on paying another's debt.
Its second warning that no soul avails another and no compensation is accepted reinforces the nontransferable final account.
Spend before a day with no trade or intercession; ordinary exchange closes before the Day's reckoning.
Believers are told to spend before a day in which there is no buying or friendship, a boundary on the market logic of debt and exchange.
Even earthfuls of gold offered as ransom are not accepted from one who dies rejecting faith, showing wealth cannot settle the final due.
All the earth and its like offered to escape the Day's punishment would not be accepted; no value can substitute for the person then.
Every wrongdoer would ransom with all the earth, but judgment is made with justice; it directly opposes a purchasable escape from account.
Wrongdoers would offer the earth and its like as ransom, yet receive the worst account and Hell: value cannot purchase a different verdict.
Possessing the earth twice over would lead wrongdoers to offer it as ransom from the evil of the Day, but the judgment exceeds such exchange.
No ransom is taken that day from hypocrites or disbelievers; the fire is their due destination.
The guilty person would like to ransom himself from that day's punishment with his children, exposing the impossible substitution of another for oneself.
He would offer his spouse and brother as ransom, extending the failed exchange to closest relations.
He would offer his clan that sheltered him, but kinship cannot discharge the personal due.
He would offer everyone on earth to save himself; the verse sets the outer limit of ransom as an answer to the section's replacement imagery.
They buy error (ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ) for guidance, and their trade does not profit: the surah's huda and dalālah become the two sides of a bad exchange.
They exchange guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment, a second explicit market scene of disastrous moral valuation.
They purchase the nearer life with the Hereafter; the transaction loses the final life for immediate value.
Those who sell Allah's covenant and their oaths for a small price have no share in the Hereafter and face punishment, joining corrupt exchange to the Day.
They purchase disbelief for faith, an explicit reversal of the profitable exchange that ends in painful punishment.
Allah purchases believers' lives and wealth for Paradise; this is the successful divine transaction opposite buying error for guidance.
It offers a trade that saves from painful punishment, deliberately answering the section's unprofitable commerce with a saving exchange.
Faith and striving are the contents of that saving trade, instead of the error and near life bought in the bad transactions.
Forgiveness and Paradise are its promised return, showing what a true recompense can be.
The command is surely occurring; it prepares 51:6's assertion that recompense is certain rather than speculative.
Recompense (ٱلدِّينَ) is surely to occur, directly confirming the inevitable Day of Recompense in 1:4.
Abraham names Allah as the one who heals him, part of his personal chain of dependence leading to the Day of Recompense in 26:82.
Abraham says Allah will cause his death and then give life, supplying resurrection for his hope about the Day in 26:82.
Abraham hopes that Allah will forgive his sin on the Day of Recompense, giving the day an individual plea for mercy as well as judgment.
On a day without doubt every soul is paid in full for what it earned and is not wronged, a compact statement of final debt settlement.
Return to Allah on a day when every soul is paid in full what it earned, and none is wronged.
Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid in full for what it did; personal standing and exact recompense coincide.
Heavens and earth are created in truth so every soul may be repaid for what it earned without injustice.
Every community is seen kneeling and called to its record; 'Today you are recompensed' fuses bodily stance, book, and account.
The earth shines, the record is set down, prophets and witnesses are brought, and judgment is made in truth without wrong.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, completing the judicial scene in 39:69.
The record leaves neither small nor great deed uncounted, and Allah wrongs no one: it is the written counterpart to an exact scale.
Each person's deed is fastened to the neck and a book is brought out on the Day of Resurrection, making personal liability visible.
'Read your book' makes the person sufficient as accountant against himself, completing 17:13's record.
On the day of presentation no secret is hidden, matching the section's claim that no one vanishes from the accounting scene.
The one given his record in the right hand announces his account, a concrete favorable settlement.
The one given his record in the left hand voices the contrary failed account.
The one given his book in the right hand receives an easy account, a formal image of merciful reckoning.
His easy accounting spells out the favorable reckoning introduced by the record in 84:7.
The one given his book behind his back receives the contrary record.
He calls for destruction, the punitive answer to the failed account of 84:10.
Two receivers sit at right and left taking down deeds, an evidentiary counterpart to written debt testimony.
No word is uttered without a ready watcher, sharpening the section's concern that account and memory not be lost.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, staging individual arrival for account.
Allah says His word is not changed and He is not unjust to servants, grounding the final verdict in fixed, even justice.
Allah informs them of what they did; they forgot it but Allah counted it, directly reversing the witness's possible forgetting in 2:282.
Allah records what people sent ahead and their traces and enumerates everything, the comprehensive ledger behind recompense.
Every soul knows what it has brought, reducing final account to the person's own presented deeds.
A person is informed that day of what he sent forward and left behind, the temporal ledger of his due.
The person remembers what he strove for when the overwhelming event comes, answering forgetfulness with recalled labor.
On that day people will be questioned about blessing, showing that even received benefit enters the account.
Allah is al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm (ٱلْقَيُّومُ), the one standing over and sustaining all things in the q-w-m sense developed by the section.
It repeats al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm, reinforcing that the one before whom creatures stand is Himself the sustainer.
Faces are humbled before the Living, Self-Subsisting One, and one bearing injustice fails; it joins Qayyūm, standing before Him, and final loss.
Allah stands maintaining justice (قَائِمًا بِٱلْقِسْطِ), a divine q-w-m expression that unites standing with the section's just balance.
Believers are told to be steadfastly standing for justice (قَوَّامِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ), turning the root's uprightness into impartial testimony.
Be standing firm for Allah as witnesses in justice, and let hostility not make you unjust; the upright stance resists a tilted verdict.
The Spirit and angels stand in rows on the day, a celestial counterpart to people standing before the Lord in 83:6.
Allah is Owner of sovereignty, giving and taking dominion; it displays the powerful disposal meant by Mālik before the Day's exclusive ownership.
Blessed is He in whose hand is all dominion and who has power over everything, illuminating the section's gloss of the king's strong hand.
In His hand is the dominion of every thing and to Him people return, bringing sovereign possession and final return together.
Dominion belongs to Allah that day and He judges between people, directly combining ملك, day, and judgment.
To Allah belongs the dominion of heavens and earth; when the Hour comes, the falsifiers lose, making earthly ownership answer to final loss.
His is the dominion on the day the trumpet is blown, another direct declaration of sovereignty at the event of judgment.
Allah is the True King, and people are not created without return to Him; true kingship entails the account denied by purposelessness.
On the day the earth is changed to another earth and people emerge before the One, Compelling Allah, غَيْر becomes a final transformation before judgment.
When skins are burned they are exchanged for other skins (غَيْرَهَا) so punishment continues; the section's 'other/replacement' sense meets divine punitive recompense.
If people turn away, Allah replaces them with another people; the verse gives غَيْر a communal substitution that warns against refusing the required response.
Whoever opens the breast to disbelief receives Allah's wrath and a great punishment, making غضب explicitly punitive.
Whoever incurs Allah's wrath falls, directly explaining wrath as an effective punishment rather than mere emotion.
One who follows Allah's pleasure is contrasted with one who incurs His wrath and whose refuge is Hell, locating wrath in final consequence.
Allah's wrath and curse are joined to Hell for hypocrites and idolaters, giving the punished sense of ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ a direct outcome.
No bearer bears another's burden, even if a heavily burdened person calls a relative; this parallels the final day when another cannot settle one's due.
No burdened soul bears another's burden, a concise boundary on transferring the moral debt of the account.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, using a financial holding image for personal liability before punishment.
Every person is held in pledge for what he earned, another debt-like image of nontransferable recompense.
The recompense of an injury is an equal injury, while pardon and reform have reward with Allah; it develops equal payment and its merciful alternative.
Retaliation must be only equivalent to what was inflicted, giving another earthly limit to measured repayment.
One who responds with the like of what he suffered is promised Allah's help if wronged again; equivalence governs retaliation here too.
The Lord gathers people and opens judgment between them in truth, a compact judicial scene under His role as decisive judge.
'This is the Day of Decision' identifies the denied event as a day of separating verdicts, close to the section's yawm al-ḥukm.
The gathered are stopped to be questioned, making the Day's judgment an interrogation as well as a weighing.
The Day of Decision has an appointed time, matching the section's day as a scheduled event more than a mere duration.
The Day of Decision is the appointed meeting of all, another formulation of the inevitable judgment day.
The angels ascend in a day measured as fifty thousand years, giving the section's 'heavy day' its Qur'anic sense of overwhelming scale.
When the trumpet is blown, the final event begins in the passage that calls it a difficult day.
It is a difficult day, directly embodying the section's severe day rather than an ordinary unit of time.
It is not easy for the disbelievers, completing the passage's severe-day contrast.
The righteous fear a day whose evil is widespread, giving moral urgency to the coming recompense.
They fear from their Lord a grim, severe day, a second explicit image of the day as crushing event.
To the Lord is the driving on that day, concentrating all movement and return under the owner of the final affair.
People are presented in rows before their Lord and told they have returned as first created, a standing-and-return scene for the account.
Every one comes to Allah individually on the Day of Resurrection, sharpening the section's personal, non-substitutable reckoning.
A people were called to a severe account and tasted the evil consequence of their affair, joining حساب to enacted recompense.
Moses seeks refuge from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account, naming the day with the section's حساب.
Forgetting the Day of Account leads to severe punishment; it turns failure to remember the reckoning into a judicial fault.
Allah will question all of them, adding direct interrogation to the reckoning image.
They will be questioned about what they used to do, completing 15:92's universal accounting.
It names the described punishment their hospitality on the Day of Recompense, another exact دِين designation for final due.
The faithful affirm the Day of Recompense, treating the section's dīn as a reality with present ethical force.
The people of the left admit that they denied the Day of Recompense, making its denial part of the path to punishment.
The sinful deny the Day of Recompense; this extends the same sūrah's fraudulent scales into the refusal of final settlement.
Denying the dīn immediately appears in conduct toward the orphan and poor, showing that denial of recompense distorts present obligations.
Inheritance is distributed only after a bequest or debt, showing that a due claim is settled before property changes hands.
Its repeated 'after bequest or debt' makes debt a prior, recorded obligation even at death.
Those burdened by debt are named among the recipients of alms, showing communal recognition of the debtor's due.
A sign is replaced or caused to be forgotten and a better or similar one brought; it gives a concrete Qur'anic instance of one thing put in another's place.
When Allah substitutes one sign for another, the verse supplies another explicit scene of replacement relevant to the section's secondary غَيْر sense.
The command to fulfill contracts supplies the broader obligation that makes debt terms and written agreements morally binding.
Trusts are returned to their owners and judgment between people is made with justice, joining owed property to upright adjudication.
On the day Allah resurrects them all, their false oaths fail before the One who knows their account; testimony cannot be manipulated then.
